      "startEvent": 927,
      "endEvent": 937,
      "contextStartEvent": 831,
      "contextEndEvent": 969,
      "speaker": "A",
      "quote": "this is a metaphysical principle that being doesn't come from non-being",
      "form": "yes",
      "substitution": "unclear",
      "protection": "no",
      "emotionalDevices": [
        "none"
      ],
      "confidence": "medium",
      "explanation": "Asked why causality extends beyond physical cases (E913–E916), Craig repeats the universal maxim; its classification alone does not establish that scope. However, he previously explains temporal becoming and explicitly offers causality as a shared assumption (E831–E893). This makes replacement of reasoning uncertain; he does not render objections inadmissible."
    },
    {
      "startEvent": 970,
      "endEvent": 976,
      "contextStartEvent": 917,
      "contextEndEvent": 989,
      "speaker": "A",
      "quote": "because it is stated as a metaphysical principle",
      "form": "unclear",
      "substitution": "yes",
      "protection": "no",
      "emotionalDevices": [
        "none"
      ],
      "confidence": "medium",
      "explanation": "After Clifton explicitly challenges reassertion of scope (E946–E969), Craig uses how the principle is stated to require justification from its challenger. That supplies no independent bridge from its formulation to its applicability. Yet this may be an ordinary burden-of-proof argument rather than a catchphrase; E977–E980 acknowledges and disputes Clifton's offered reason."
    }
  ],
  "contrasts": [
    {
      "startEvent": 1270,
      "endEvent": 1288,
      "speaker": "A",
      "quote": "The Kalam argument is just neutral as to whether every event has a cause.",
      "explanation": "Craig distinguishes the argument's commitment about things beginning to exist from a separate claim about every event, and identifies libertarian freedom as an additional issue. The concise conclusion summarizes an explicit qualification."
    },
    {
      "startEvent": 208,
      "endEvent": 240,
      "speaker": "B",
      "quote": "Whatever has an efficient cause of its existence has a material cause.",
      "explanation": "Clifton supplies an alternative principle to test whether induction discriminates between rival claims. He presents the resulting inference conditionally, acknowledges possible reasons for rejecting it, and calls for a tiebreaker rather than treating the maxim as settled proof."
    }
  ]
